claims.text: The coating has a well-dispersed dual-phase microstructure containing FCC and BCC regions.
The FCC/BCC interfaces are coherent or semi-coherent.
The dual-phase microstructure imparts superior creep resistance.
Interfaces between FCC and BCC phases act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Lattice mismatch at FCC/BCC phase boundaries generates back-stress.
Interface-generated back-stress slows progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading.
Constant stress at elevated temperature promotes creep behavior in the coating.
Approximately 600°C is below the temperature at which phase instability or coarsening may occur.
Lattice-parameter and strain mismatch at FCC/BCC interfaces impedes dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion delays plastic flow and reduces creep strain rate.
The dual-phase coating will have a statistically significant lower creep strain rate than a comparable predominantly single-phase coating.
Post-creep characterization of the dual-phase coating will reveal dislocation pile-ups at FCC/BCC interfaces.
Post-creep characterization will reveal interface-related strain fields that are absent or diminished in the single-phase baseline.
The proposed interface-barrier mechanism is effective only below the threshold for phase coarsening or interface destabilization.
The proposed mechanism is effective only below stresses that induce phase transformation or rapid damage accumulation.
The magnitude of phase-boundary back-stress relative to other strengthening mechanisms may vary with composition and processing history.
